title: Unpaid in Hawaii; staying and marrying
summary: The leader C. P. Johnson had taken the band's pay in advance because of a narcotics charge; Young stayed in Hawaii and married there.

story.theme_name: Meeting, marrying and raising a family
story.community_name: Meeting, courting and marrying: musicians' love lives

blocks.x: And this was in '47. And most of them, we -- in fact, we didn't get paid because, when we went, we didn't know that C. P. Johnson, the leader, had a narcotics charge on him here, back here in L. A., so he'd written and gotten most of the money advanced so he could get enough, buy enough time to go over there and do those jobs.

So we got over there. We played a week. We didn't get no pay. And we know the people were making money. So one of the promoters seemed to be a pretty good joe, so they picked up all our tabs. You know, we didn't have any tabs, and we had our plane tickets back.

But so we asked him, say what about our money? You know, C. P., you never could catch him to talk business with him. He said, why I sent your money in advance. We say, what do you mean in advance? He says, well, we sent the money to C. P. They didn't never know C. P. had no -- C. P. told them that the band wouldn't leave L. A. without being paid in advance.
So they sent him this money, you know. Wasn't a
whole lot of money, because we weren't making a whole lot from the gig. But whatever it was, you know, it was our salaries for the first week. And he says, oh, no, we didn't get no money from him.

So then we found out later that C. P. had this narcotic charge on him in L. A., and he used the money so he could get -- buy enough time to get away, you know, to do these things. He came right back, and we didn't get no pay. And we worked another week, no pay. We worked about three weeks without getting paid, and so some of the guys wanted to turn him into the union. I said, for what? The guy has no money.

Red and I, we didn't turn him in to the union. So we stayed around there, and Red and I, we all had our tickets back, but the other guys came back. And Red stayed for a while, and there was another, a piano player with us, he doesn't live here anymore -- he lives up around -- his name was Bracken, Warren Bracken.

And he was a pretty good piano player, because when we were over there (inaudible) Vivian Dandridge came over there to do a job at another club. We didn't play for her, but we got -- we met her and got -- I knew her, in fact, and he got to going with Vivian. That's how I remember Bracken.
Well, he was going with Vivian, and they left and came back together. But Red and I stayed. And later on Red

left, but I still stayed over there. So -- and I wound up -- I went there for six weeks. I wound up getting married over there, and I stayed for about -- I don't know -- I stayed for about six -- until I went with Louis -- '47 -- I went with Louis in '52.
